title: Lal Ded — a season of the tradition's women
hook: a boat hauled across the sea on a rope of loose thread, and water seeping from an unbaked cup: Lal Ded admits she might not make it

segments.voice: Yesterday, Lal Ded: the bride with a stone under her rice, and the one word her teacher gave her, from outside, go within.

A cup shaped from wet clay and dried in the sun, but never fired in a kiln. It looks like a cup. It holds its shape. Pour water in, though, and the sides darken. Drop by drop, the water soaks into the clay and seeps away, and the cup begins to soften. In one saying Lal Ded uses that kind of cup to describe herself, next to an even shakier picture: a boat, a whole sea, and a rope of loose thread.
screen: `A CUP OF UNBAKED CLAY.` → `THE WATER SEEPS AWAY.` → `A BOAT ON A ROPE OF THREAD.`

segments.voice: Here is the vakh, in paraphrase. With a rope of loose, untwisted thread, I am hauling a boat across the sea. If only God would hear me and carry me over. Like water in cups of unbaked clay, I am seeping away. How I long to go home. Take the pictures one at a time. First the rope. A boat on the open sea is heavy, and the water pulls against it; towing it with untwisted thread is close to hopeless. The rope is whatever she has to pull with: her effort, her discipline, her practice. She doesn't pretend it's strong. Then the prayer in the middle: if only God would hear me. She isn't boasting that she's arrived. She's asking to be carried. Then the cup, her life draining away a little each day, the way water leaves unfired clay. Then the last word, home. Not the house she left. Some Shaiva readers in Kashmir hear the self finding its way back to Shiva, its true home; some hear, more simply, the ache to be where you belong. Notice the honesty. The woman who danced free on one word, remembered as a teacher, says plainly: my rope is weak, my time is leaking, I may not make it across on my own. The tradition kept this saying. It didn't polish it into a victory. It let a saint say she was struggling.
screen: `A ROPE OF LOOSE THREAD` · `A BOAT ACROSS THE SEA` · `WATER IN UNBAKED CLAY` · `THE LONGING FOR HOME`

segments.voice: Bring to mind one thing you're trying to pull across a wide stretch of water, a habit, a hard conversation, a hope, and look without blame at what you're pulling with, thin or frayed; then keep pulling anyway. If you pray, you can ask in your own words to be carried the rest of the way. And if the rope ever feels too thin to hold, you don't have to pull alone: in the US, call or text 988, or reach your local emergency number.
Lal Ded. The poet hauling a boat with loose thread, seeping away like water in unbaked clay, and still longing for home. Today's word.
